proposals.statement: The co-op has multiple information sources that are not easily accessible for growers to track their fruit status and payments

evidence.quote: the growers. They phone us all day. Where's my fruit, what was my packout, when do I get paid, why did my bins get downgraded? And we can't answer them quickly, because the information is in, I'd say, five different places. And some of it is on paper.

proposals.statement: The co-op uses a carbon copy delivery ticket system with handwritten entries for grower information

evidence.quote: The truck goes over the weighbridge, and our clerk writes a delivery ticket. It's a carbon book, three copies. White copy for the grower, pink for the office, yellow stays in the book.

Handwritten. The weighbridge has a little computer with the scale program on it, it's called WeighMate, and it prints the weight on a slip. Then the clerk copies the weight onto the ticket, with the grower number, the farm, the orchard block, the cultivar and the number of bins.

proposals.statement: The co-op uses an optical grader system that sorts citrus into classes and generates packout reports

evidence.quote: Then the bins go onto the line. We've got an optical grader, the Optisort, that photographs every fruit and sorts it into classes. Class one for export, class two for the local market, and then juice. The grader's computer makes a report for each batch. A batch is basically one delivery ticket.
And the report says how many cartons of each class and the percentages. That's what we call the packout.

proposals.statement: The co-op uses a spreadsheet for monthly calculations of advance payments to growers

evidence.quote: So the spreadsheet is, uh, the heart of the whole thing, unfortunately. Every delivery is a row. Marietjie types in the ticket from the pink copy, and then she adds the packout from the grader report. And then at the end of each month I use that to work out the advance payments to the growers.
My spreadsheet. Well, it's the co-op's spreadsheet, but I built it.

proposals.statement: The co-op has a slow process for processing deliveries due to manual steps and waiting periods

evidence.quote: It depends. In the peak, sometimes two days. The early mandarins have to go through degreening first, in the rooms at the back, so it can be a while. The oranges usually go the next day.

proposals.statement: The co-op has a complex payment system with advance payments and a final pool payment that is difficult to track

evidence.quote: So in citrus you don't get paid the full price when you deliver. The fruit gets exported, it goes on a ship, it gets sold in Rotterdam or wherever, and only months later do we know the final price. So we pay the growers an advance. So much per carton of class one, so much per carton of class two, a few rand per bin of juice.
After the season there's a final pool payment, when all the money is in.

proposals.statement: The co-op has a manual process for generating payment statements for growers

evidence.quote: They get a statement. I make it in the spreadsheet, and Marietjie prints it and posts it, or emails it to those who have email. Some of them still come and collect it at the office, they like to have a cup of tea with her.

proposals.statement: Growers receive payment statements three weeks after the month ends due to manual typing, checking, and reconciliation with the bank

evidence.quote: Um, honestly, three weeks. Sometimes more. Because everything has to be typed first, and checked, and then I have to reconcile with the bank.

proposals.statement: Growers experience confusion about packout percentages due to manual handling of cardboard tags that fall off or have incorrect ticket numbers

evidence.quote: Because when a batch packs out badly, the grower thinks we made a mistake. He thinks his bins got mixed up with someone else's. And sometimes, to be honest, they did. Because the cardboard tag fell off, or the ticket number was written badly and someone read a seven as a one.

proposals.statement: Marietjie types for three to four hours daily in the season, and she is retiring at the end of June next year, which is mid-season
